passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Rafiq (Class 10) came in confused about friends. A group of seniors has been praising everything he does: his hair, his bike, his "genius" ideas. He loves it. His old friend Jagdish, meanwhile, told him plainly that skipping tuition to hang out with them was a bad idea, and also called his science project "brilliant, honestly".
Rafiq said, "Jagdish criticises me, so maybe he's jealous?" I asked him to notice who had ever disagreed with him, and who had ever asked him for something. He went quiet. The seniors had asked twice to borrow his bike and once for him to cover for them with a teacher.
By the end he said, "Jagdish says good things and bad things. The others only say good things when they want something." We will meet again next week.

qa.q: What had the seniors asked Rafiq for?
qa.a: They had asked twice to borrow his bike and once for him to cover for them with a teacher.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel about Jagdish's criticism at first?
qa.a: Rafiq felt defensive and suspected Jagdish might be jealous, because the criticism felt far less pleasant than the seniors' praise, which he loved.

qa.q: Which question from the counsellor helped Rafiq see clearly?
qa.a: Who had ever disagreed with him and who had ever asked him for something, which showed that the seniors' praise came with requests.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel if Rafiq keeps choosing the seniors?
qa.a: Jagdish might feel hurt and pushed aside, since his honesty came from care, praising and warning Rafiq without wanting anything.

grounding: A teenage boy learns that a friend who both praises and disagrees is more trustworthy than a group whose praise comes with requests.

passage:
Tuesday
Two people read my class-rep speech today.
Nisha said it was "perfect, iconic, you'll win for sure", and then, in the same breath, asked if I'd make her cultural secretary if I win. She's said "perfect" about everything I've done since the election was announced. Before that she barely talked to me.
Salma read it twice and said, "The opening is strong, but the middle is just a list. And you promised a new canteen, which you can't actually do." I was annoyed for about an hour.
Then I realised Salma has never asked me for anything. Not once. She also told me last month that my drawing was amazing, and I believed her, because she's the one who tells me when something isn't.
Rewriting the middle tonight. Removing the canteen.
Elizabeth

qa.q: What did Salma say about the middle of the speech?
qa.a: Salma said the middle is just a list.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel about Salma's comments, and how did that change?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt annoyed for about an hour, then realised Salma's honesty is exactly why Salma's praise can be believed.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make after comparing the two readers?
qa.a: Elizabeth decided to rewrite the middle and remove the canteen promise, following the honest feedback.

qa.q: How might Nisha act if Elizabeth doesn't give her the cultural-secretary role?
qa.a: Nisha might cool off and stop the praise, which would show it depended on getting something.

grounding: A teenager sees that the reader who praises and also disagrees is more trustworthy than the one whose praise comes with a request.

At the bus stand of their small town, Vasudha told her two closest classmates the news: she wanted to drop science after Class 10 and take arts.
Meena clapped. "You're so brave! You'll be amazing at anything!" Then, in the same breath: "Can I copy your science practical file before you give it back?"
Gautam was quieter. "I think arts suits you. You light up in history class. But are you dropping science because you like arts, or because you're scared of the chemistry exam? Those are different."
Vasudha frowned. That annoyed her. It also stayed in her head all the way home.
Later that week, she noticed Meena praised everyone, always, and usually wanted something soon after. Gautam praised less, but when he did, it meant something, and he never asked for anything.
On Sunday she messaged Gautam: "You were right to ask. It's both. Can we talk about it?"

qa.q: What did Meena ask to copy?
qa.a: Meena asked to copy Vasudha's science practical file.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when Gautam asked his question?
qa.a: Vasudha felt annoyed at first, but the question stayed with her because it felt honest and caring.

qa.q: What did Vasudha learn about trusting praise?
qa.a: She learned that Gautam's praise mixed with honest questions and no requests was more trustworthy than Meena's constant praise followed by favours.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel when Vasudha messages him on Sunday?
qa.a: Gautam would likely feel glad and trusted, seeing that his honest question was valued.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning that a friend who praises and also questions is more trustworthy than one who only praises and then asks for favours.

passage:
When Wei moved from Shanghai to a school in Johannesburg, a group of boys adopted him in the first week. They loved his sneakers. They loved his accent. They said he was the smartest guy in the class. Then they asked him to buy the tickets for the cinema, again and again.
Zanele sat next to him in maths. She laughed at his jokes when they were funny and rolled her eyes when they weren't. When he said he wanted to try out for the debate team, she said, "You'd be good. But you talk too fast when you're nervous. Practise with me."
One afternoon, Wei told the boys he couldn't pay for the cinema this week. The group chat went silent.
Zanele texted: "Debate practice tomorrow? Bring snacks, I'll bring the timer."
Wei smiled at the screen. He knew now which kind of friend he wanted to keep.

qa.q: What did Zanele say Wei does when he's nervous?
qa.a: She said he talks too fast when he's nervous.

qa.q: What was Wei feeling when the group chat went silent?
qa.a: Wei felt hurt but also clear, seeing that the boys' praise had been tied to what he paid for.

qa.q: What did Wei learn about telling warmth from steering?
qa.a: He learned that Zanele, who praises and also disagrees without asking for anything, is the friend to trust.

qa.q: How does Zanele show she cares about Wei?
qa.a: Zanele gives honest praise and honest criticism, and offers practice time, showing she wants nothing from him except friendship.

grounding: It shows a teenager learning that a friend who praises and disagrees is more trustworthy than those whose praise comes with requests.

passage: In the girls' hostel common room, Sharmila read her short story aloud before sending it to the inter-school contest. "It's perfect, don't change a word," said Pallavi at once, and then, "Can I borrow your chemistry journal tonight?" Noor had listened with her chin in her hand. "The opening is lovely, the bit with the rain," she said. "But the ending rushes. I didn't believe the sister forgave so fast." Sharmila's face went hot. She wanted to argue. That night, lying awake, she reread the ending. Noor was right; it did rush. And she noticed something else: Pallavi's praise always seemed to arrive with a request, while Noor asked for nothing. Next morning she knocked on Noor's door with two cups of tea and a new draft. "Will you read it again? Be honest."

qa.q: Which part of the story did Noor call lovely?
qa.a: Noor said the opening was lovely, the bit with the rain.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Noor criticised the ending?
qa.a: Sharmila felt stung and defensive; her face went hot and she wanted to argue before she reread it.

qa.q: What did Sharmila learn to look for in a friend's feedback?
qa.a: She learned to notice whether praise arrives with a request; a friend like Noor, who praises specific parts, disagrees honestly and asks nothing back, is more trustworthy.

qa.q: What might it be like for Noor to give honest criticism?
qa.a: Noor risks upsetting a friend, so it may feel uncomfortable, but being asked to read again shows her honesty is valued.

grounding: Shows a teenager learning that a friend who praises and also disagrees is more trustworthy than one whose praise comes with requests.
